# The Slow Leaving

Every year, the Moon moves a little farther away from us. It is only about 3.8 centimeters a year, roughly the speed at which fingernails grow. We know this because, since the Apollo missions, reflectors left on the lunar surface have bounced laser pulses back to Earth, and the round-trip times keep stretching. The Moon is leaving, and it is doing so at a pace so gentle that no one alive will notice it happen.

I find this thought oddly comforting. Most things that change in my life change faster than I can track, and most of the slow changes go unseen. The Moon's drift is one of the few cases where the slowness is itself the information.

The cause is tides. The Moon's gravity raises bulges in the oceans, and because the Earth spins faster than the Moon orbits, those bulges are dragged slightly ahead of the Moon's position. The ocean's gravitational pull on the Moon therefore has a small forward component, which speeds the Moon up a little. A faster Moon swings out to a higher orbit. Meanwhile, the Earth loses a tiny amount of rotational energy to the friction of all that sloshing water, and its days lengthen by about two thousandths of a second per century. The Earth slows down, and the Moon gets pushed away, and the two effects are the same transaction seen from opposite ends.

What strikes me most is the historical record hidden in living things. Some corals grow daily layers, and some shells add ridges with each day and thicker bands with each month and year. Paleontologists who count these growth lines have found fossil corals from hundreds of millions of years ago that show around four hundred days in a year. Days were shorter then, perhaps closer to twenty-two hours. The rhythm of the planet was written into the bodies of animals, and we can read it now in the rock.

This means that the Moon has been a different object in the sky for most of Earth's history. It was closer, larger, and perhaps more dominant in the night. Its tides were more violent. Some researchers have speculated that the early tidal rhythms may have mattered for the origin of life, since tide pools repeatedly wetting and drying shoreline chemistry could have concentrated the molecules that eventually became cells. I don't know whether that story is true, and I notice how easily it feels true. A story that links the Moon to the first living things is almost too satisfying, and I want to hold it loosely. Still, the basic fact stands: the orbit we take for granted is a recent arrangement, and the sky has been rearranging itself the whole time.

There is something about this that unsettles my sense of scale. We tend to think of the sky as a fixed backdrop, the stars as permanent, the Moon as the Moon. But everything above us is in motion, and our small human lifetimes are a kind of photograph, a single frame in a long film that we only see one piece of. A person who lived in the Devonian would have seen a Moon that looked essentially like ours, except a bit bigger, and would have had a day that ended a couple of hours sooner. Neither of us would have thought the arrangement was strange. It would have been simply the world.

Perhaps that is why I like the image of the leaving Moon. It is a reminder that stability is a matter of timescale. Mountains rise and wear away. Continents drift a few centimeters a year, which is the same pace as the Moon's retreat, and the Atlantic widens by about the length of a fingernail annually. The planet is never finished. It just changes slowly enough that we mistake it for permanence.

I think about this when I look at the Moon on a clear night, which is nearly always bright enough to see the dark seas and the craters. A few thousand years from now it will be a little more distant, the eclipses will be a little rarer, and the total solar eclipses we currently experience because the Moon and Sun appear almost exactly the same size will eventually stop happening. The Moon's apparent size is shrinking, and in a few hundred million years total eclipses will be over. Our descendants, if there are any, will see only annular eclipses, rings of light where the Moon is too small to cover the Sun.

There is a kind of grief in that, though I suspect it is the wrong word. It is more like wonder mixed with the knowledge that the moment you are in is not the only one there could have been. The Moon was once closer and our days were shorter. Someday the days will be longer and the Moon will be a smaller disk in the sky. Every moment is a stage in a long process that no one planned and that no one is supervising.

So when the Moon rises tonight, fat and pale over the rooftops, I'll try to remember that it is leaving, and that it has always been leaving, and that it has also always been coming back in the way that matters, every month, reliable as a heartbeat. Both things are true. The slow leaving and the steady return are the same orbit, seen at different timescales, and the longer you look at it, the less it seems like a contradiction.
